Bart Weetjens founded a unique lab in Tanzania dedicated to training rats to sniff out deadly unexploded land mines — the legacy of countless bloody conflicts. Although dogs had traditionally been used to help humans detect mines, Weetjens, who had long felt a special bond with rodents, realized that African giant pouched rats were lighter, cheaper to care for, and less susceptible to tropical disease.

In “Hero Rats,” FRONTLINE/World reporter Alexis Bloom accompanied Weetjens to neighboring Mozambique to watch his organization’s trained rodents in action. She also visited a school there that was cleared of landmines with the help of the rats, allowing the children to resume their education and play without fear of stepping on a mine. The rats save human lives, Weetjens said, “and, yes, they are heroes, actually.”

items.title: How This $140M Company Sold Shares of Homes It Didn't Own | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Remy and Jean-Marc Jacobson said they wanted to revolutionize the real estate industry when they launched their crypto company, RealToken, in 2019. This July, they announced that they will be liquidating the company’s $140 million portfolio. 

The company bought over 700 properties across the United States using limited liability companies and sold shares – or tokens – in those companies exclusively to foreign investors across the blockchain. Thousands of investors across the world now have their money stuck in these tokens with little to no recourse. 

Issues with RealToken’s properties in Detroit – which makes up 75 percent of its U.S. portfolio – first came to light when the City of Detroit sued the company and the Jacobsons in July of 2025, alleging that they violated local housing regulations.

The city’s complaint included exhibits showing the dilapidated conditions of the homes – standing sewage in basements, black mold on walls, crumbling infrastructure – which it called harmful to the health and safety of the public. 

Over the course of eight months, The Journal investigated how the company operated in Michigan and in its second largest market, Ohio, combing through public records and financial documents. We found that not only were hundreds of homes in disrepair, but that RealToken paid investors from properties that were vacant or that they did not even own, leading investors to ask: was this a scam or a venture gone wrong?

items.title: Morocco's cannabis reform: Why small farmers are left behind | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Morocco's legalization of cannabis for medicinal purposes was welcomed by growers in the country. The promise of a better future, however, has yet to materialize for many small-scale farmers.

Cannabis farmers in northern Morocco are under pressure from changing climate conditions, with water shortages intensifying the already fierce competition in the sector. In Azila, a village that depends entirely on the drug trade for its livelihood, farmers are allowed to cultivate cannabis but are not authorized to trade it. Here in the Rif Mountains, thousands of families rely on cannabis cultivation, but most live under precarious conditions. The most productive land, where the plants grow best, belongs to a handful of large operators who are increasingly taking control of the business. Anyone who continues to sell the crop illegally risks imprisonment.
Many farmers support legalization because they hope it will enable them to live without a constant fear of prosecution. The government's legalization program, however, is progressing more slowly than expected, with fewer farmers than anticipated taking part.
The push for legalization was driven by the medical uses of cannabis. The cannabis plant contains more than one hundred cannabinoids. The best known is THC, which alters the taker's perception, concentration and sense of time, but can also trigger mental health problems. CBD, by contrast, has calming, relaxing, and anti-inflammatory effects without causing intoxication.
The legal pharmaceutical production of cannabis is subject to strict regulations, mandatory quality standards, and comprehensive inspections - requirements that discourage many small-scale farmers.
At the same time, there is widespread distrust of state institutions. Many people complain about arbitrary treatment and corruption. Police officers who profit from the illegal trade undermine the implementation of the reforms. 
This documentary explores the promises and pitfalls of cannabis legalization for Morocco's cannabis-growing communities - where the debate itself often divides generations and even families.

items.title: Will non-alcoholic wine save the winemakers? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Wine consumption is declining in Europe. This poses a threat to European wine-growing regions. Winemakers in Spain and Germany are seeking a way out of the crisis by producing alcohol-free wine.

Many people want to live healthier lives. As a result, alcohol consumption in Europe has declined: by a good 20 percent, over the past 20 years. It’s a trend that also impacts wine: Experts warn that nearly a third of Germany’s vineyard acreage could disappear in the coming years. Particularly affected are the labor-intensive steep slopes. These slopes produce distinctive wines, shape the cultural landscape and attract tourists.

Jürgen and Luca Dahms share their love of wine. Yet their perspectives also diverge. Father Jürgen, a winemaker, stands for classic, traditional wine enjoyment, while Luca, who works in the insurance industry, has found surprising success marketing alcohol-free wines. Both see an opportunity to preserve threatened vineyards by de-alcoholizing wines. 

In Spain, in the historic wine region of Toro, winemaker Iván Alonso Gil is undertaking a bold experiment. His full-bodied red wines come from ancient vines. items.author: French Cooking Academy
items.content:
<article>The majority of cooks struggle with even the simplest baking recipes and it almost always comes down to a fundamental conflict in mindset and method.

In this video, we are leaving the cooking mindset at the door and put our bakers hat on to bake a classic French staple: the famous Gâteau au Yaourt (Yogurt Cake). This foolproof, ultra-moist cake is the ultimate building block for any home cook that has given up on baking and wants to build real baking confidence!

Ingredients Ratio (Gâteau au Yaourt)

Uses a standard 150g / 5.3oz yogurt pot as the unit of measurement:
1 pot Plain Yogurt (150g / 5.3oz)
2 pots Fine White Sugar (300g / ~1 ½ cups)
3 pots Self-Raising Cake Flour (225g / ~2 cups)
Note: If using standard cake flour, add 2 tsp baking powder.
1 pot Neutral Vegetable Oil (150ml / ~⅔ cup)
3 Medium Eggs (at room temperature)
1 tsp Vanilla Extract 

Oven Settings & Timing: Bake at 180°C / 350°F Conventional Heat (or 160°C / 320°F Fan-Forced) for roughly 40 to 50 minutes—the cake is ready when a knife inserted into the center comes out clean!

 Video Chapters
0:00 - Why Cooks Struggle With Baking
1:32 - The French Solution: Gâteau au Yaourt
2:04 - Step 1: Setting Up Your Space Like a Baker
3:03 - Step 2: The Ingredients & The "Wrong Flour" Trap

💡 Key Takeaways For Cooks
Ditch the All-Purpose Flour: Use Cake Flour for a light, tender crumb instead of a heavy brick.

Of Pakistan's 240 million people, 47 percent are under the age of 18. Yet, economic stagnation and a weak education system are fueling frustration among the country’s young and rapidly growing population.
 
Against this backdrop, the military has considerably expanded its influence in what political analysts say is a "hybrid" system of governance with elected civilian representatives. The military continues to play a major role in the country's politics and economy. While the human rights organizations criticize the army's role in politics, the military officials point to various security challenges that, in their view, require their involvement.

When the United States took control of Venezuela's oil exports in early 2026, it collected an estimated $13 billion in crude sales — but the official ledger in Caracas records almost none of it, and six months on there is still no public accounting of where the money went. In this video we look at what happened to Venezuela's sovereign wealth: the missing oil revenues now sitting in an offshore account in Qatar, the four billion dollars of Venezuelan gold frozen in the vaults of the Bank of England that no one can legally claim, and the court-ordered auction that handed Citgo's parent company to an affiliate of Paul Singer's Elliott Management for nearly $6 billion. Along the way we explain the legal machinery that makes all of this possible — the alter ego doctrine, sovereign immunity and the Bancec ruling, the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, and the "one voice" principle in English law — and the broader lesson for anyone trying to understand sovereign assets: a nation's wealth held abroad is only yours for as long as someone else's courts, banks and vaults agree that it is. items.title: By train to Mount Etna | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For almost 120 years, the "Circumetnea” narrow-gauge railway has been circling Europe’s highest volcano. The train travels through impressive lava landscapes and vegetation zones, as well as two nature parks, with the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Mount Etna always in view.

At the foot of Mount Etna, amidst black rocks and prickly pears, the narrow-gauge railway winds its way through rocky wastelands, wooded areas and lush green hills. Lava eruptions have meant the railway line has had to be rebuilt many times over the years, most recently in 1981. Mount Etna, standing at 3,352 meters, is Europe’s most active volcano. Most eruptions affect mainly the immediate vicinity of the crater; they rarely pose a threat to people or animals. However, violent eruptions do occur from time to time. Then, volcano spews clouds of ash and chunks of rock kilometers into the atmosphere, and lava flows make their way down into the valley.

Following the closure of the railway network in Sicily, the Circumetnea Railway is the island’s last remaining narrow-gauge railway. The journey from Catania to the terminus at Riposto takes three hours. Winding its way through lava fields that resemble lunar landscapes and past deserted stations, the train travels more than 100 kilometers to its terminus on the Ionian Sea.

items.content:
<article>One of the most contested issues in astrophysics is our understanding of the Universe’s expansion. Nobel laureate Adam Riess discusses why there is disagreement and what might resolve it.

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time. One of the biggest mysteries in cosmology seems to keep getting bigger. Astronomers have known since the 1930s that the universe is expanding, but in the 1990s, the discovery that this expansion is accelerating rather than slowing down came as a huge shock to the field. Something had to be driving that acceleration, and dark energy was proposed as the cause. What began as a seismic shock in cosmology eventually led to a Nobel prize.

But this story has a sequel, and it comes with another major plot twist. The two main methods for estimating the universe's present-day expansion rate are producing significantly different answers. As a result, how fast the universe is really expanding has become a matter of considerable debate — with no small amount of angst — and the discrepancy has become known as the Hubble tension. Perhaps most surprising of all is that one of the loudest voices raising concern is Adam Riess, the astrophysicist whose Nobel Prize-winning work helped ignite the acceleration debate in the first place.

Riess joined co-host Steven Strogatz on The Joy of Why to explain how we got to this point, what the Hubble tension might be telling us, and what may happen next.

DESCRIPTION
Joanna Bryson challenges many popular assumptions about AI and AGI. She argues that current generative AI systems are not autonomous intelligences but powerful tools that compress and reproduce human cultural knowledge at scale. While these systems can appear intelligent, they remain dependent on human-created data, corporate incentives, and carefully engineered guardrails. Bryson cautions against anthropomorphizing AI and emphasizes that many concerns about AI stem from misunderstandings about how these systems actually work.

The discussion ultimately centers on responsibility and governance. Bryson argues that transparency, accountability, and democratic oversight matter far more than debates about machine consciousness. Whether discussing AI companions, recommendation algorithms, open-source models, regulation, or AI-assisted software development, her conclusion remains consistent: technology is not destiny. Engineers, companies, policymakers, and citizens all have agency in shaping how AI is deployed, regulated, and integrated into society. [...]
